description: In two centuries, Italy reinvented painting, sculpture, and architecture, and changed the way we see the world.

hero.hook: In two centuries, Italy reinvented art and the way we look at the world.

blocks.text: The Italian Renaissance (14th to 16th century) was not only a change of style. It was a new way of seeing the world. In two centuries, Italy put observation, reason, and the individual at the center of everything.

Born in the wealthy cities of the peninsula, this revolution reinvented painting, sculpture, and architecture. Two engines drove it: the rediscovery of Greek and Roman antiquity, and a run of bold technical inventions.

It all began in **Florence**, which dominated the European economy in the 14th century through cloth and banking. The **Medici** family took power there. These bankers used [[patronage]], the funding of artists, as a tool of prestige.
To get around the ban on lending at interest, the Medici invented clever banking tricks. The Church looked the other way as long as they kept paying for chapels.

blocks.caption: Lorenzo de' Medici, known as “the Magnificent,” a great protector of artists

blocks.text: At the same time, **humanism** changed the place of man. Thinkers like [[Pico della Mirandola]] argued that a human being can understand nature through reason. In **1453**, the fall of Constantinople pushed scholars toward Italy, carrying forgotten Greek manuscripts with them.

sections.title: Florence, the city that lit the fuse

blocks.text: In the 15th century, the architect **Brunelleschi** invented [[linear perspective]] around **1420**. Gone was the medieval habit of painting important things bigger. Space now followed mathematical rules, like a window opened onto the real world.

blocks.caption: Perspective gives the illusion of depth on a flat surface

blocks.text: **Leonardo da Vinci** pushed further. He dissected bodies to understand muscle and nerve, and to paint emotion as well. Oil paint, which came from Flanders, slowly replaced [[tempera]] and made [[chiaroscuro]] possible: those contrasts of light and shadow that give a figure real depth.
The body Leonardo studied most closely belonged to a man of a hundred. Examining him, he described one of the first known cases of an artery blocked by old age.

sections.title: Painting the real: perspective and the body

blocks.text: At the start of the 16th century, Rome took Florence's place, carried by building popes like **Julius II**. This was the age of the “complete man.” **Leonardo da Vinci** was the model: painter, engineer, anatomist.

**Michelangelo** stands for force. His **David** became the symbol of Florence. Between **1508** and **1512**, he painted the ceiling of the **Sistine Chapel**: 500 square meters on the book of Genesis.

blocks.caption: Michelangelo, from the David to the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel

blocks.text: In *The Last Judgment*, Michelangelo painted his own face on a flayed skin: his way of saying how far the work had worn him out.
**Raphael** stands for grace. His fresco *The School of Athens* gathers the great thinkers of antiquity in a harmony that served as a model for centuries.

After Raphael died in **1520**, the balance came apart. Artists stretched their figures and pushed their colors: this was [[mannerism]], a more anxious kind of art. The French king **Francis I** invited Leonardo north and launched the **French Renaissance**, with the châteaux of the Loire.

blocks.text: Born in Florence thanks to the Medici, the Italian Renaissance transformed art with perspective (around 1420) and the study of the body, before reaching its peak in Rome with Leonardo, Michelangelo, and Raphael.
